title: Jaundice after a holiday — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

blocks.text: Jaundice after a holiday — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

Round 5 • PACES Station 2: acute consultation • Skills C communication, E clinical judgement, F managing concerns, G welfare (with focused A/B/D where relevant) • 20 minutes • Educational examiner-style encounter • Prepared 14 October 2026 • Not an official PACES mark scheme

A 32-year-old presents with yellow eyes, dark urine and fatigue after international travel. Take a focused history, identify serious liver dysfunction and discuss investigations and public-health implications.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Acute hepatitis, with hepatitis A or E among the travel-associated possibilities. Trap: Elevated INR with encephalopathy indicates possible acute liver failure and urgent transplant-centre discussion; assess pregnancy because hepatitis E may be especially severe. Notify public health for suspected hepatitis A and consider contact vaccination by UKHSA risk assessment.

rows: “First I need to check if this is affecting your immediate safety.”
“I have a working diagnosis but need to exclude dangerous alternatives.”
Hepatitis B/C, drug injury (including paracetamol), biliary obstruction, autoimmune hepatitis and haemolysis require exclusion according to pattern.
Several infections and non-infectious problems can cause jaundice. We will check liver function, clotting and specific tests before labelling this hepatitis A or E.

Assess observations, encephalopathy, bleeding, hydration; send LFTs, bilirubin, INR/PT, FBC, U&E, glucose, HAV IgM, HEV serology/RNA as appropriate, HBV/HCV tests and ultrasound if obstruction suspected. Supportive care and specialist review if severe.
Hand hygiene matters. If hepatitis A is confirmed or suspected we will involve public health, who decide whether close contacts need vaccination or immunoglobulin.
Check patient priorities, understanding and follow-up.
Adapts pace, autonomy and escalation to distress.
Elicits time-course and key red flags.
Uses discriminating positives/negatives to focus testing.

Assess mental state, INR/PT, glucose and physiological stability urgently; encephalopathy with impaired synthetic function suggests acute liver failure and needs immediate specialist liver-centre discussion. Screen for paracetamol and other drug toxicity, viral hepatitis A/E/B, and pregnancy if relevant; do not anchor on travel alone.

States rationale, checks contraindications and escalation context; Danger: encephalopathy, coagulopathy or hypoglycaemia; refer urgently, avoiding delayed escalation for viral serology. For acute liver failure (coagulopathy with INR above 1.5 plus any encephalopathy), discusses early with a liver transplant centre and uses the King’s College criteria for prognosis (EASL 2017).
Tests delay treatment or miss severity.
Sequences tests without postponing lifesaving care.
Dismisses fears or uses unexplained jargon.

blocks.text: Opening line: “I have turned yellow after travelling. Could my family catch this?” The actor is concerned but able to engage unless the examiner introduces deterioration. Release only history in the candidate brief; do not volunteer a diagnostic label. Ask “Why do you need to do that?” after proposed treatment. Acknowledge clear, compassionate explanations.
Available observations/findings: Jaundice, fatigue, nausea, dark urine and recent travel; no current confusion. No laboratory diagnosis has yet been made.

Q1 Examiner: “What is your working diagnosis?”  Model response: Acute hepatitis, with hepatitis A or E among the travel-associated possibilities.
MODEL (corrected critical decision): Assess mental state, INR/PT, glucose and physiological stability urgently; encephalopathy with impaired synthetic function suggests acute liver failure and needs immediate specialist liver-centre discussion. Screen for paracetamol and other drug toxicity, viral hepatitis A/E/B, and pregnancy if relevant; do not anchor on travel alone.

Q2 Examiner: “What important alternative must remain in view?”  Model response: Hepatitis B/C, drug injury (including paracetamol), biliary obstruction, autoimmune hepatitis and haemolysis require exclusion according to pattern.

Q3 Examiner: “What initial action and tests are required?”  Model response: Assess observations, encephalopathy, bleeding, hydration; send LFTs, bilirubin, INR/PT, FBC, U&E, glucose, HAV IgM, HEV serology/RNA as appropriate, HBV/HCV tests and ultrasound if obstruction suspected. Supportive care and specialist review if severe.

Q4 Examiner: “What is the most dangerous mistake?”  Model response: Elevated INR with encephalopathy indicates possible acute liver failure and urgent transplant-centre discussion; assess pregnancy because hepatitis E may be especially severe. Notify public health for suspected hepatitis A and consider contact vaccination by UKHSA risk assessment.
Q5 Examiner: “What is the first severity discriminator?”  Model response: INR and mental state, alongside glucose and evidence of acute liver failure.
Q6 Examiner: “Which transmission patterns differ?”  Model response: HAV and HEV are often faecal–oral; HEV can involve undercooked meat in the UK as well as travel.
Q7 Examiner: “Do all household contacts receive immunoglobulin?”  Model response: No; UKHSA assesses exposure, immunity and eligibility; vaccination is the mainstay.
Curveball: the patient becomes hypotensive or less responsive. Stop the routine consultation, call for help and reassess ABCDE; this is not a test of a rote differential list.
• [R1 G] Identifies unstable patient and obtains support.
• [R2 C] Obtains discriminating history and patient priorities.
• [R3 D/E] Gives justified working diagnosis and alternatives.
• [R4 E] Orders time-critical tests without treatment delay.
• [R5 E] States named treatment and safety restriction.
• [R6 C/F/G] Explains, checks understanding and gives preventive advice.

FAIL — CANDIDATE: “This is probably nothing urgent; let us wait for all the results.” [R1 Fail; R5 Fail] PATIENT: “But I am frightened.” CANDIDATE: “We have no time for that.” [R6 Fail] EXAMINER: “What is your diagnosis and differential?” CANDIDATE: “I cannot say.” [R2–R4 Fail] Examiner note: poor safety, reasoning and communication.

PASS — CANDIDATE: “I can see you are worried. I will assess your observations now and call the right team if you are unwell.” [R1 Pass; R6 Pass] PATIENT: “I have turned yellow after travelling. Could my family catch this?” CANDIDATE: “I need to establish the onset, risks and associated symptoms before deciding.” [R2 Pass] EXAMINER: “Your impression?” CANDIDATE: “Acute hepatitis, with hepatitis A or E among the travel-associated possibilities. Hepatitis B/C, drug injury (including paracetamol), biliary obstruction, autoimmune hepatitis and haemolysis require exclusion according to pattern.” [R3 Pass] EXAMINER: “Next step?” CANDIDATE: “Assess observations, encephalopathy, bleeding, hydration; send LFTs, bilirubin, INR/PT, FBC, U&E, glucose, HAV IgM, HEV serology/RNA as appropriate, HBV/HCV tests and ultrasound if obstruction suspected. Supportive care and specialist review if severe.” [R4 Pass; R5 Pass] CANDIDATE: “Several infections and non-infectious problems can cause jaundice. We will check liver function, clotting and specific tests before labelling this hepatitis A or E.” [R6 Pass] Examiner note: safe structured approach.

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “I will assess your stability while keeping you informed; please tell me what worries you most.” [R1 High-performance; R6 High-performance] PATIENT: “I have turned yellow after travelling. Could my family catch this?” CANDIDATE: “I would clarify timing, trigger, associated symptoms and medication/exposure details that discriminate serious causes.” [R2 High-performance] EXAMINER: “What makes this urgent?” CANDIDATE: “Acute hepatitis, with hepatitis A or E among the travel-associated possibilities. However, Hepatitis B/C, drug injury (including paracetamol), biliary obstruction, autoimmune hepatitis and haemolysis require exclusion according to pattern.” [R3 High-performance] EXAMINER: “What happens now?” CANDIDATE: “Elevated INR with encephalopathy indicates possible acute liver failure and urgent transplant-centre discussion; assess pregnancy because hepatitis E may be especially severe. Notify public health for suspected hepatitis A and consider contact vaccination by UKHSA risk assessment. My priority investigation and treatment plan is: Assess observations, encephalopathy, bleeding, hydration; send LFTs, bilirubin, INR/PT, FBC, U&E, glucose, HAV IgM, HEV serology/RNA as appropriate, HBV/HCV tests and ultrasound if obstruction suspected. Supportive care and specialist review if severe.” [R4 High-performance; R5 High-performance] PATIENT: “What about after today?” CANDIDATE: “Hand hygiene matters. If hepatitis A is confirmed or suspected we will involve public health, who decide whether close contacts need vaccination or immunoglobulin. Could you tell me your understanding, so I can correct anything unclear?” [R6 High-performance] Examiner note: explicitly prioritises harm, engages the person and provides anticipatory advice.

R2/R3: Missing the characteristic pattern or treating a suggested cause as proven. Hepatitis B/C, drug injury (including paracetamol), biliary obstruction, autoimmune hepatitis and haemolysis require exclusion according to pattern.

R4/R5: Omitting the named critical action. Elevated INR with encephalopathy indicates possible acute liver failure and urgent transplant-centre discussion; assess pregnancy because hepatitis E may be especially severe. Notify public health for suspected hepatitis A and consider contact vaccination by UKHSA risk assessment.
R6: Saying “we will monitor” without a comprehensible explanation of what is being done.
“I will check whether this patient is physiologically unstable before proceeding.”

“The key safety issue is: Elevated INR with encephalopathy indicates possible acute liver failure and urgent transplant-centre discussion; assess pregnancy because hepatitis E may be especially severe. Notify public health for suspected hepatitis A and consider contact vaccination by UKHSA risk assessment.”
“Let me explain why the next investigation and treatment cannot wait.”

Clinical correction,— Assess mental state, INR/PT, glucose and physiological stability urgently; encephalopathy with impaired synthetic function suggests acute liver failure and needs immediate specialist liver-centre discussion. Screen for paracetamol and other drug toxicity, viral hepatitis A/E/B, and pregnancy if relevant; do not anchor on travel alone. Acute liver failure is coagulopathy (INR above 1.5) plus any encephalopathy: discuss early with a liver transplant centre and use the King’s College criteria for prognosis (EASL 2017).

THINK: Acute hepatitis, with hepatitis A or E among the travel-associated possibilities. SAY: Several infections and non-infectious problems can cause jaundice. We will check liver function, clotting and specific tests before labelling this hepatitis A or E. DO: Assess observations, encephalopathy, bleeding, hydration; send LFTs, bilirubin, INR/PT, FBC, U&E, glucose, HAV IgM, HEV serology/RNA as appropriate, HBV/HCV tests and ultrasound if obstruction suspected. Supportive care and specialist review if severe. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: Elevated INR with encephalopathy indicates possible acute liver failure and urgent transplant-centre discussion; assess pregnancy because hepatitis E may be especially severe. Notify public health for suspected hepatitis A and consider contact vaccination by UKHSA risk assessment. FINISH: Hand hygiene matters. If hepatitis A is confirmed or suspected we will involve public health, who decide whether close contacts need vaccination or immunoglobulin.
